caption:
Miss the "no interest" end date, and the interest can go back to the day you bought it.

WHY: many store-card deals in the US and Canada say "no interest if paid in full in 12 months". That is often deferred interest. If any of the price is still unpaid when the promotion ends, interest can be charged on the whole purchase, back to day one, not just on what's left.

THE CFPB'S NUMBERS: a $400 TV on a 12-month deal. You pay $25 a month, so $300. $100 is left at the end. At a 25% rate, $65 of interest from the past year lands on top: you owe $165, not $100.

HOW (5 minutes, when you sign up):
1. Find the exact end date on the agreement or your statement. Write it in your phone calendar.
2. Divide the price by the number of months. $400 / 12 is about $34 a month (math). Pay at least that every month. The minimum payment is usually not enough.
3. Have other balances on the card? Ask the card company to put your extra payments on the promotional balance.

THE CATCH: terms differ. Some plans charge interest only on what's left, some on the full amount from the purchase date, and some lose the 0% after one missed payment. Read your plan's terms. Your plan's real rate may be higher or lower than 25%.

WHO THIS IS FOR: anyone in the US or Canada using a store card or "buy now, pay later" plan with a no-interest period.

Do this: divide the price by the months and pay at least that, every month.

Send this to a friend who just bought something on a store card.

Education only, not financial advice.

Follow for one money rule a day, in plain words.

#deferredinterest #creditcards #moneytips #personalfinance #buynowpaylater

Sources (checked Oct 27, 2026):
• US: CFPB, 'How to understand special promotional financing offers on credit cards' (consumerfinance.gov/archive/blog/how-understand-special-promotional-financing-offers-credit-cards/): with deferred interest, if you don't pay off the entire promotional balance, 'interest going back to the date of the purchase will be added'; the $400 TV, $25 a month, 25% rate, $65 interest, 'you will owe $165'; the minimum payment is usually not enough to pay it off in time; you can ask to have extra payments applied to the promotional balance.
• Canada: FCAC, 'Buy now, pay later plans' (canada.ca/en/financial-consumer-agency/services/loans/buy-now-pay-later.html): retail credit cards may offer promotional rates as low as 0%; missing a payment or not paying in full by the due date may lose the promotional rate; depending on plan terms, interest may be charged on the full amount from the date of purchase or on the unpaid balance.
• Math: $400 / 12 = $33.33, so about $34 a month clears it before the end date.

caption:
Card bill 30 days late? It can stay on your credit report for up to 6 years in Canada and 7 in the US.

WHY: lenders look at your payment history when you apply for a loan, a car, a rental or a mortgage. In Canada, a late or unpaid credit card or loan can stay on your report for up to 6 years. In the US, most negative information can be reported for 7 years. A payment that hits 30 days late this month can stay until 2032 in Canada and 2033 in the US.

Paying it later doesn't erase it: the late mark stays even after you pay the past-due amount.

HOW (5 minutes tonight):
1. Open your card's app or online banking.
2. Find autopay (it may be called automatic or pre-authorized payments).
3. Set it to at least the minimum payment, on or before the due date. If you can, set it to the full balance so you pay no interest.

THE CATCH: a payment a few days late usually costs a late fee, but it generally isn't reported to the credit bureaus until it's 30 or more days past due. So if you just missed one, pay it today. Autopay only works if the money is in your account; a failed payment can cost a fee from your card company and your bank.

WHO THIS IS FOR: anyone with a credit card or loan in Canada or the US.

Do this: turn on autopay for at least the minimum payment.

Send this to a friend who pays their bills by hand.

Education only, not financial advice.

Follow for one money rule a day, in plain words.

Sources (checked Oct 27, 2026):
• Canada: FCAC, 'How long information stays on your credit report' (canada.ca/en/financial-consumer-agency/services/credit-reports-score/information-credit-report.html, modified 2026-07-01): 'information about late or unpaid credit cards and loans: up to 6 years.'
• Canada: Equifax Canada, 'How long does information stay on your credit report?' (equifax.ca): 'Late payments remain on a credit report for up to 6 years from the date reported' and 'remain… even if you pay the past-due balance.'
• US: CFPB, 'How long does information stay on my credit report?' (consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/…-en-323/, reviewed Sep 2, 2026): 'A credit reporting company generally can report most negative information for seven years'; accurate negative information such as late payments can't be removed.
• Canada: TransUnion Canada, 'Understanding your Consumer Disclosure' (ocs.transunion.ca/ocs/understanding.html): the first late payment rating is '2 - Overdue 30-59 days' (then 60-89, 90-119, 120+).
• US: Equifax, 'When does a late credit card payment show up on credit reports?' (equifax.com): late payments 'generally won't end up on your credit reports for at least 30 days after the date you miss the payment'; once reported, they stay seven years.
• Math: late in 2026 + 6 years = 2032 (Canada, upper limit); + 7 years = 2033 (US).
